The notes below cover only what the pages I read actually said.

## Notes on Matthew 18

**v. 1**
- The disciples seem to have argued about rank and then asked Jesus to settle it. They probably pictured an earthly kingdom with top posts to give out (Guzik, citing Poole and Trapp). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/
- Ellicott: Mark and Luke say they had been arguing on the road. The promise to Peter and the choice of three disciples to see the Transfiguration may have stirred up rival claims. Benson: this happened just after Jesus foretold His death, which shows how worldly their hopes still were. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/18-1.htm
- Poole rejects the idea that Peter's keys (16:19) caused the argument. If only Peter had been given the keys, the question would already have been settled, so the keys must have been given to all equally. Same URL.
- **Protestant view of Peter:** Guzik says that if Peter were the first pope as Roman Catholic teaching holds, Jesus should have named Peter the greatest here. He doesn't. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/

**v. 2**
- Jesus could have pointed to Himself. Instead He pointed to a child. That the child came when called says something about what Jesus was like (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/
- There is a tradition that the child grew up to be Ignatius of Antioch. Guzik gives it through Barclay and Clarke, and Clarke calls its source unreliable. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/ Ellicott says this is a late Eastern Church tradition that rests on misreading Ignatius's title "Theophoros." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/18.htm

**v. 3**
- In that culture children had no status. Carson (quoted by Guzik) says the child stands for humility and indifference to status, not for innocence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/
- **Traditions differ on what "converted/change" means:**
  - Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary say it is not "conversion" in the later technical sense of turning from habitual sin. It means turning away from ambition. https://biblehub.com/matthew/18-3.htm
  - Benson, a Methodist following Wesley, reads it as turning from worldly aims. He adds, while doubting the text itself says this much, that full inner renewal is needed to enter glory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/18-3.htm
  - Calvin ties the "conversion" to the child example: the disciples must go a completely different way from ordinary human habits. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/18-3.html
  - Precept Austin takes the verb as a full change of life's direction. Oswald Chambers, quoted there, ties it to the new birth and a new nature. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-18-commentary
- Barnes: Jesus was not commenting on whether children are morally good by nature. He meant only that disciples must drop pride and ambition. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/18-3.html

**v. 4**
- To humble yourself means accepting a lower position, as Christ did (Phil 2:8). It does not mean fake modesty (France, quoted by Guzik). Spurgeon: children are humble without trying, and copied humility is off-putting. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/
- Barnes: "greatest" means the most eminent Christian, the one with most of the true spirit of faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/18-5.html

**v. 5**
- Ellicott sees this as the first statement of the judgment principle in Matt 25:40. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/18-5.htm
- The "child" here stands for a humble disciple (Calvin, Barnes, Constable). Receiving such a person for Jesus' sake counts as receiving Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/18-5.html
- Spurgeon: to bless a little one is to host the Saviour himself. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-18-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 6**
- The "little ones" are true disciples of any age who trust like children. The passage is not only about literal children. https://www.gotquestions.org/little-ones.html
- The word means a large millstone turned by a donkey, not a hand mill. Drowning was not a Jewish punishment. Ellicott says its worst horror was that the body got no burial. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/18-6.htm
- Calvin reads the verse as comfort for humble believers whom the world looks down on. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom32.ii.lix.html
- Coffman: the worse-than-drowning fate is eternal death. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/18-6.html

**v. 7**
- The first "woe" expresses pity and the second is a warning. Those who cause the stumbling have no excuse, and God will deal with them, so the wronged can let go of bitterness (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/
- **A difference in emphasis:**
  - Clarke (labelled Wesleyan/Arminian on studylight) says offences are unavoidable because people are wicked and stubborn. Both the one who causes the offence and the one who takes it are in danger. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/18-7.html
  - Matthew Henry says God allows offences for wise and holy purposes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/18-7.htm GotQuestions also points to God's sovereignty: offences show which faith is real and which is fake. https://www.gotquestions.org/offenses-must-come.html
  - Ellicott holds both truths together: sin keeps recurring almost like a law, yet each offender chose freely and is responsible. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/18-7.htm
- Spurgeon: proud people are the main cause of stumbling. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64327/

**vv. 8–9**
- Not to be taken literally. Cutting off a limb doesn't go far enough, because a person can still sin with the other hand, or in the heart. What is needed is inner change (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/ The studylight commentators (Smith, Contending for the Faith, Light of Israel) agree it is deliberate exaggeration. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/18-8.html
- Barnes: the resurrection body will not be maimed. The picture just means it is better to give up what leads to sin than to be lost. Gill links this to Matt 5:29–30. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/18-8.htm

**v. 10**
- Guzik: the verse is often read as being about "guardian angels." Angels do minister to believers (Heb 1:14), but there is no need to limit this to one angel per person. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/
- Chuck Smith takes it as angels keeping watch over children before the Father. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/18-6.html

**v. 11**
- Guzik quotes the verse as part of his text but says nothing about the manuscripts. I found no comment on the textual question.

**vv. 12–13**
- This is a different parable from Luke 15, with a different purpose (Carson, quoted by Guzik). Spurgeon warns against looking down on someone because they are only one person, because they are small, or because they have strayed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/

**v. 14**
- Guzik: some read this as assurance that children who die before the age of accountability are saved. He says that is certain only for believers' children (1 Cor 7:14). For others we trust God's mercy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/

**v. 15**
- Go to the person directly rather than gossiping. Guzik says you may also simply bear with it patiently. It is enough at first that "he hears you." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/

**v. 16**
- The extra witnesses may find that the blame lies differently than the first person thought (Prov 18:17). Restoration matters more than being proved right (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/
- Biblehub links this to Deut 19:15. https://biblehub.com/matthew/18.htm

**v. 17**
- Guzik says to treat the person as you would a pagan, with love aimed at bringing them back. He links this to 1 Cor 5. France notes that no leaders or elders are named. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/
- Biblehub: the purpose of withdrawal is to wake the conscience. https://biblehub.com/matthew/18.htm

**v. 18**
- Bruce (quoted by Guzik) says binding and loosing means judging conduct, here treating a sin as forgivable or not. Spurgeon (Baptist) says each church holds the keys of its own door, and heaven confirms what the congregation does rightly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/
- Biblehub says the words echo rabbinic terms for forbidding and permitting. https://biblehub.com/matthew/18.htm
- I could not reach Catholic or Lutheran sources on this verse.

**v. 19**
- Guzik (Enduring Word, which falls under your Pentecostal/charismatic heading) teaches that there is "exponential" power in agreeing together in prayer, based on Lev 26:8. Spurgeon is more cautious: God sometimes answers what lies behind our prayers rather than the exact words. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/

**v. 20**
- Large numbers, rank, place and form don't matter; meeting in Jesus' name does. Clarke says only God could truly say these words, because only God is everywhere present (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/

**vv. 21–22**
- Peter's "seven" was generous, because rabbis suggested three times. Jesus' answer removes the limit altogether. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/
- Spurgeon says it doesn't matter whether you read 77 or 490, since an indefinite number is meant. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64327/ Matthew Henry: it looks bad to keep count of offences. https://studylight.org/commentaries/mhm/matthew-18.html

**vv. 23–34**
- Biblehub's summary: the parable sets a debt that could never be paid against a trivial one. https://biblehub.com/matthew/18.htm
- Haydock (Catholic) says the 10,000 talents fit, because any grave offence against God hugely outweighs offences against people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/18-35.html
- MacArthur says the key phrase is "I forgave you all that debt" (v. 32): the forgiveness was real. https://www.gty.org/sermons/2335/learning-to-forgive-part-3

**v. 35** (traditions really differ here)
- **MacArthur (gty):** Jesus is speaking to true believers. Unforgiveness brings God's chastening; the passage is not about losing salvation. Unbelievers cannot forgive this way at all. https://www.gty.org/sermons/2335/learning-to-forgive-part-3
- **Matthew Henry:** God does not forgive and then charge the guilt again later. The ending exposes people who wrongly assume they are forgiven but never knew the gospel's grace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/18-35.htm
- **Ellicott:** he leans toward a conditional reading. The marks of pardon appear or fade with the forgiven person's faith and love. Same URL.
- **Guzik:** forgiving others is evidence of being forgiven. We should forgive without waiting for the other person to repent, because we are forgiven sinners and not in God's position. Forgiving does not cancel legal consequences. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-18/
- **Others on studylight:** Coffman says no one can be saved without a forgiving heart. Constable says this is not earning forgiveness. McGee says this is "not quite the basis" for believers' forgiveness today. Haydock (Catholic) says forgiveness must be real and give up all wish for revenge. Ellicott says "their trespasses" is missing from some of the best manuscripts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/18-35.html

---

To fill the gaps, the next searches would be netbible.org on vv. 11, 22 and 24, Lutheran (lcms.org) and Catholic (catholic.com) sources on v. 18, and Enduring Word and biblehub on vv. 23–34.
